findings.title: Password verification can be bypassed when using a backup code
findings.body: The password check at line 121 is conditioned on `!credentials.totpCode`. An attacker who knows a valid backup code can send a request with any non-empty `totpCode` value (e.g., "000000") along with the valid `backupCode`. Because `totpCode` is non-empty, the password verification is skipped entirely. Then at line 131, the condition `user.twoFactorEnabled && credentials.backupCode` is true, so the backup code path is taken and the user is authenticated without ever verifying the password. The `totpCode` value is never validated in this path. To fix, the password check should not be skipped when a backup code is being used, or the condition should be refined to only skip the password check in the legitimate external TOTP flow (e.g., by checking a separate flag or ensuring the request originates from the SAML/Google redirect).

findings.title: Race condition allows a backup code to be used more than once
findings.body: The backup code consumption follows a read-modify-write pattern (read encrypted codes at line 139, find index at line 144, set to null at line 148, write back at line 149-156) without any locking or atomic operation. If two concurrent login requests arrive with the same valid backup code, both can read the code before either writes the null, allowing the same backup code to be used twice. This undermines the one-time-use guarantee stated in the UI ("Each backup code can be used exactly once"). Consider using a database-level atomic update or a transaction with row-level locking.

findings.title: Backup codes are persisted before 2FA setup is completed
findings.body: The setup endpoint stores backup codes in the database (line 68) immediately after password verification, before the user has confirmed the TOTP code in the subsequent enable step. If the user abandons the setup flow (closes the modal without entering the TOTP code), orphaned backup codes remain in the database with `twoFactorEnabled: false`. While they cannot be used for login (since 2FA is not enabled), they represent unnecessary sensitive data at rest. Consider deferring the backup code storage to the enable step, or cleaning them up if setup is abandoned.

findings.title: Client-side minLength allows submission of codes without dash that may confuse users
findings.body: The input has `minLength={10}` which permits a 10-character input without the dash (e.g., "abcde12345"). While the server strips dashes with `replaceAll("-", "")` and would accept this, the placeholder shows "XXXXX-XXXXX" format. More importantly, HTML `minLength`/`maxLength` validation only fires on form submission in some browsers and does not prevent programmatic submission via react-hook-form. If the intent is to enforce the dashed format on the client, additional validation (e.g., a pattern attribute or react-hook-form validation rule) would be needed.
